interviewQuestions.question: Tell me about a time you led a decision that affected more than just your own team.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'll use a case where two teams were both building against the same shared data model with slightly different assumptions, which was quietly causing data quality bugs neither team could fully explain on their own.

I decided we needed a single written ownership boundary rather than each team patching around the ambiguity independently — that was my call to make, not something I was asked to do. I ran a working session with both teams' leads, proposed a specific split of responsibilities, and got both engineering managers to sign off on a short doc that became the reference going forward.

The result: the class of bug stopped recurring, and the doc got reused as a template when a third team ran into a similar ambiguous-ownership situation six months later. I'd frame my own contribution precisely — I decided we needed the doc and drove the alignment process; the two teams did the actual implementation work to conform to it.

What I'd emphasize if pushed: the hard part wasn't writing the doc, it was getting two teams with different priorities to agree to a boundary that meant extra work for at least one of them in the short term.

**Testing:** whether your answer demonstrates cross-team scope and precise ownership language, not just a well-told individual contribution.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Cross-org scope

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide which stories to lead with when you're interviewing for a level above your current title?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I go through my existing story bank and explicitly flag which ones are honestly scoped at the target level versus my current one, rather than assuming every good story automatically qualifies.

Most engineers, even before a formal promotion, have at least one or two genuine higher-scope moments — covering for an absent lead during a launch, driving a decision across teams because no one else stepped up, mentoring someone into a role I used to hold. I keep those specifically earmarked, because loops interviewing for the next level often include a probe along the lines of 'show me you're ready for more' and I want a real answer on hand rather than stretching a same-level story to sound bigger than it was.

For the rest of my stories that are honestly still at my current scope, I don't discard them — they're still valid answers to conflict, failure, or ambiguity questions — but I'm conscious not to let all of my answers cluster at my current level, since a pattern of only current-scope stories across a whole loop is itself a signal, even if each individual story is fine.

What I explicitly avoid is exaggerating scope on a story that wasn't actually that big — an interviewer's follow-ups tend to expose that within a couple of questions.

**Testing:** whether you can honestly self-assess scope across your own story bank rather than either underselling your real reach or inflating stories to fit a level you haven't demonstrated yet.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Self-assessment

interviewQuestions.question: You said 'we decided' a lot in that last answer. Can you be specific about what you personally did?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Fair pushback, and I'd answer it directly rather than getting defensive, because this is exactly the kind of follow-up that separates precise ownership language from vague team-credit language.

Going back to the story: the specific decision to consolidate two overlapping services was mine — I proposed it, built the initial cost-benefit case, and took it to both team leads. What the team did, once I'd made that case and gotten buy-in, was the actual migration work: writing the new interface, running the phased cutover, handling the edge cases that came up. I said 'we decided' because by the time we executed, the team had genuinely bought in and shaped the details — but the initial call and the case for it were mine.

I'd rather over-clarify this distinction than let 'we' quietly blur into taking collective credit for a decision I made alone, or the reverse — undercutting my own contribution by hiding behind 'we' when I should say 'I.'

This is a habit I've had to build deliberately: default to 'I decided, and here's how the team executed' rather than either pure 'I' or pure 'we,' because it's the most accurate description of what actually happened in most real team decisions.

**Testing:** whether you can immediately disambiguate 'I' versus 'we' under direct pressure, rather than retreating into vague collective language when challenged.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Precision under follow-up

interviewQuestions.question: As someone early in their career, how would you approach a behavioral question that seems to expect a bigger story than you actually have?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd tell the honest, appropriately-scoped story rather than reaching for something bigger than what actually happened — an accurate individual-scope answer is stronger than a stretched or borrowed one.

For example, if asked about resolving a disagreement and my real experience is a disagreement with one teammate over a code review approach, I'd tell that story well: what I proposed, why, how I explained the reasoning, and that the PR merged with the relationship intact. I wouldn't try to inflate it into something involving multiple teams that didn't actually happen, because a follow-up question almost always exposes the gap between a real story and a padded one.

What I would do is make sure the story is told with real precision — the specific technical reasoning, the specific moment the teammate came around, not vague summary — since depth at the appropriate scope reads much better than a shallow attempt at a bigger scope. I also keep an eye out for the rare moments where I did operate above my usual scope, even early on, like the one time I helped onboard a new hire faster than expected, and I keep that ready in case a question calls for it.

**Testing:** whether you understand that scope should match your honest level rather than being artificially inflated, and that a well-told, correctly-scoped story outperforms an exaggerated one every time a follow-up probes it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Honest scoping
